Abstract:   Anomaly detection is a longstanding and active research area that has many applications in domains such as finance, secur-
ity and manufacturing. However, the efficiency and performance of anomaly detection algorithms are challenged by the large-scale, high-
dimensional and heterogeneous data that are prevalent in the era of big data. Isolation-based unsupervised anomaly detection is a novel
and effective approach for identifying anomalies in data. It relies on the idea that anomalies are few and different from normal instances,
and thus can be easily isolated by random partitioning. Isolation-based methods have several advantages over existing methods, such as
low computational complexity, low memory usage, high scalability, robustness to noise and irrelevant features, and no need for prior
knowledge or heavy parameter tuning. In this survey, we review the state-of-the-art isolation-based anomaly detection methods, includ-
ing their data partitioning strategies, anomaly score functions, and algorithmic details. We also discuss some extensions and applica-
tions of isolation-based methods in different scenarios, such as detecting anomalies in streaming data, time series, trajectory and image
datasets. Finally, we identify some open challenges and future directions for isolation-based anomaly detection research.
Keywords:   Isolation forest, isolation kernel, anomaly detection, isolation-based methods, machine learning.

 1   Introduction
Anomaly detection refers to the identification of data
points  that  significantly  differ  from  the  normal  patterns
in  a  dataset[1, 2].  The  study  of  anomalies  in  data  dates
back to the 19th century in statistics[3]. In recent years,
anomaly detection has been a crucial task in various re-
search  and  industrial  domains,  such  as  health  care[4, 5],
finance[6, 7],  security[8, 9],  energy[10, 11] and  manufactur-
ing[12–14],  where  it  can  help  monitor,  control  and  secure
various processes and systems.
Anomaly  detection  methods  can  be  broadly  categor-
ized into two main classes based on whether neural net-
works are used for feature learning, i.e., shallow methods
and  deep  methods.  Additionally,  these  methods  can  be
further classified according to their modelling approaches
into one-class classification, probabilistic-based, distance-
based  and  reconstruction-based  categories[15].  Each  ap-
proach  has  distinct  strengths  and  limitations,  requiring
careful  selection  based  on  specific  application  scenarios
and requirements.
In recent years, self-supervised learning methods based
on  deep  neural  networks  have  gained  significant  atten-
tion  and  demonstrated  strong  performance  in  anomaly
detection[5].  Although  these  methods  do  not  require  la-
belled data, they often rely on complex data augmenta-
tion  strategies  and  pseudo-label  generation,  demanding
extensive  computational  resources  and  large-scale  train-
ing[16, 17].
In this paper, we focus on anomaly detection methods
that  rely  on  isolation  mechanisms,  which  belong  to  the
shallow distance-based category. Compared to deep learn-
ing  approaches,  isolation-based  methods  provide  a  light-
weight and computationally efficient alternative, particu-
larly  suitable  for  real-world  scenarios  requiring  high
timeliness, strong interpretability and compatibility with
edge  deployment  or  industrial  applications[18].  Isolation-
based  methods  operate  exclusively  in  an  unsupervised
learning  setting,  where  no  labelled  data  or  prior  know-
ledge of anomalies are required[19]. By leveraging the stat-
istical  or  structural  properties  of  data,  isolation-based
methods can detect anomalies directly from deviations in
the data′s inherent characteristics, making them ideal for

The core idea of isolation-based methods is to employ
an isolation mechanism that constructs partitions in the
input data space, such that anomalies are more likely to
be isolated from the majority of the data[19]. The first and
most  representative  method  in  this  family  is  isolation
forest  (iForest)[19].  Following  its  success,  various  exten-
sions  and  improvements  have  been  proposed  to  address
specific  challenges  and  enhance  performance,  including
isolation-based anomaly detection using nearest-neighbor
ensembles  (iNNE)[21],  extended  isolation  forest[20],  Opti-
Forest[22],  and  isolation  distributional  kernel[23].  Notably,
these  methods  are  designed  to  detect  anomalies  without
requiring any learning.
This paper is the first comprehensive survey of isola-
tion-based unsupervised anomaly detection. It reviews the
anomaly  detection  methods  based  on  isolation  mechan-
isms,  covering  their  data  partitioning,  anomaly  scoring
and algorithmic aspects. It also explores some extensions
and  applications  of  isolation-based  methods  for  various
scenarios, such as streaming data, time series, trajectory
and image datasets. Lastly, it highlights some open chal-
lenges and future directions.
 2   Anomaly definition
An anomaly is an observation that significantly devi-
ates from some concepts of normality[24]. Fig. 1 shows the
6  kinds  of  anomalies  on  different  datasets  and  they  can
be broadly categorized as follows:
1)  Point  anomalies are  individual  instances  that
differ markedly from the majority of the data[1].
2) Group or collective anomalies are a subset of
data points that exhibit anomalous behavior as a whole
compared to the rest of the data[26–28].
3) Contextual or conditional anomalies are data
points  or  groups  that  are  only  anomalous  in  a  specific
context or condition[1, 15].
For unstructured data such as images and texts, an-
omalies can be distinguished at two levels as follows[15, 29]:
1)  Low-level  sensory  anomalies are  data  in-
stances  that  differ  from  the  expected  low-level  features,
which  correspond  to  pixel-level  characteristics,  such  as
texture defects or artifacts in images.
2)  High-level  semantic  anomalies are  data  in-
stances  that  violate  the  expected  high-level  features,
which  correspond  to  semantic  concepts  or  topics  in  the
text, such as the class of the object.
All  the  reviewed  isolation-based  anomaly  detection
methods  in  this  paper  operate  under  the  unsupervised
setting, where the training data is entirely unlabelled, and
no  data  augmentation  or  pseudo-label  is  needed[19].  Un-
like  supervised  or  semi-supervised  methods  that  rely  on
labelled anomalies or partially labelled datasets, isolation-
based  methods  are  designed  to  detect  anomalies  purely
based  on  their  statistical  or  structural  properties  in  the
data.  This  assumption  aligns  with  the  practical  reality
that  labelled  anomaly  samples  are  often  rare,  expensive
to  obtain,  or  even  unavailable  in  many  real-world
scenarios[2].

into rectangles (or hyper-rectangles in higher dimensions),

dom forest chooses a feature and a threshold that maxim-
ize  the  information  gain  or  minimize  the  Gini  impurity,
which  depend  on  the  class  labels  of  the  data  points.

 3.2   Non-axis parallel splitting
The  axis-parallel  splitting  of  data  space  can  cause  a
specific  limitation,  i.e.,  it  obscures  anomalies  that  align
with the axes of normal data clusters[21, 30]. To overcome
this issue, many non-axis parallel splitting strategies have
been proposed.
 3.2.1   Random hyperplane
SCiForest  uses  random  hyperplanes  to  replace  axis
parallel splitting to partition the data space in isolation
forest[31]. Random hyperplanes are similar to oblique hy-
perplanes  which  have  been  studied  in  the  decision  tree,
both  of  them  are  non-axis  parallel  to  the  original
feature[32]. The difference between them is that the attrib-
utes  and  coefficients  are  chosen  randomly  in  SCiForest,
but  they  are  chosen  to  minimize  the  impurity  based  on
labels in an oblique decision tree.

Summary. Isolation  partitioning  strategies  differ  in
their ability to isolate anomalies effectively under differ-
ent scenarios. Axis-parallel splitting, as used in the stand-
ard isolation forest, is computationally efficient due to its
simplicity,  but  it  struggles  to  capture  anomalies  aligned
with  the  axes  of  normal  data  clusters.  Random  hyper-
planes,  employed  by  SCiForest,  address  this  limitation
through  oblique  splits,  enabling  more  flexible  isolation,
but  the  use  of  random  projections  adds  slight  computa-
tional  overhead.  Hash-based  splitting,  introduced  in
LSHiForest,  leverages  LSH  to  group  similar  points  into
bins, extending binary trees into multi-fork trees based on
hash bins. This approach generalizes the isolation mech-
anism to work with diverse distance measures, data types
and spaces where LSH families are defined. However, its
effectiveness depends on the choice of LSH family and as-
sociated  parameters,  which  may  require  careful  tuning.
Hyperspheres and Voronoi diagrams in iNNE and aNNE
algorithms adapt to local density patterns, effectively en-
abling the detection of local anomalies in sparse regions.

most  of  the  other  points,  which  are  considered  normal.

 4.3   Other applications
The above mentioned methods can be directly used in
many academic and industrial fields with static, numeric-
al and structured data, such as sensors[38–40], network se-
curity[41, 42],  finance[43],  medicine[44–46] and  energy[47, 48].
They can also be applied to other types of datasets as fol-

 4.3.1   Streaming data
Streaming  data  are  independent  and  identically  dis-
tributed (i.i.d.) and have several distinctive features, such
as real-time processing requirements, continuous flow, se-
quential ordering, large data volumes and theoretically in-
finite  duration[49, 50].  Most  streaming  anomaly  detection
algorithms  are  based  on  static  anomaly  detectors,  but
with  additional  mechanisms  to  handle  the  dynamic
nature of streaming data. These algorithms usually con-
sist of two components: an anomaly detector that assigns
anomaly scores to the incoming data points, and a model
updater  that  adapts  the  underlying  model  to  the  chan-
ging data characteristics.
Isolation-based methods have been commonly used as
the  static  anomaly  detector  in  some  streaming  anomaly
algorithms, e.g., IDForest[51], iForestASD[52], HS-Trees[53],
RRCF[54],  etc.  A  common  procedure  used  in  streaming
anomaly detection algorithms is as follows: 1) An initial
model  is  trained  on  some  data;  2)  new  data  points  are
scored as they arrive; 3) since streaming data may exhib-
it concept drift[50], which refers to the change in data dis-

 8   Discussions and prospects
 8.1   Isolation mechanisms applied to tasks
not related to anomaly detection
Since  the  concept  of  isolation  was  introduced,  it  has
not been confined to point and group anomaly detection
only.  The  isolation  mechanism  has  been  applied  to  nu-
merous other tasks, including:
1)  Clustering:  A  new  class  of  clustering  algorithm
based on point-set kernel can cluster a massive number of
points  in  a  few  minutes  linear  time  complexity,  e.g.,
psKC[95], StreaKHC[96], TIDKC[97] and IDKC[98].
2)  Emerging  new  class  detection:  A  task  which  is
seemingly  unrelated  to  anomaly  detection,  but  has  been
shown  that  it  can  be  addressed  effectively  using  an
isolation-based  anomaly  detector,  i.e.,  emerging  new
class[99, 100].
3) Classification: Multi-instance learning[101] and graph
classification via isolation graph kernel[83].
4) Kernel estimators and regression: Ting et al.[102, 103]
proposed a novel approach for density estimation and re-
gression  using  isolation  kernels,  which  enables  adaptive
kernel  density  estimator  (IKDE)  and  kernel  regression
(IKR) with constant-time complexity for each estimation.
This means that the resulting estimators have the same
computational complexity as the original isolation kernel,
making  them  the  first  KDE  and  KR  that  are  both  fast
and adaptive.
5)  Change-point/interval  detection:  Isolation-based
change  interval  detector  (iCID)[93] can  identify  different
types of change-points in streaming data with the toler-
ance of outliers and linear time complexity.
6) Topological data analysis: A newly proposed kernel-
based  filter  function[104],  inspired  by  isolation  kernel,
demonstrates robustness against noise and varying densit-
ies within a point cloud for topological data analysis.

There are some open challenges and future directions
for isolation-based methods as follows.
 8.2.1   Theoretical 
analysis

different isolation mechanisms. How to directly calculate

scalability and responsiveness.
 8.2.2   Incremental learning
For streaming data, most isolation-based methods re-
build  the  model  from  scratch  when  new  data  comes,
which is inefficient and impractical for large or fast data
streams.  Incremental  learning  techniques  are  needed  to
update  the  models  without  losing  accuracy  or  adding
much computation.
 8.2.3   Partitioning optimization
Partitioning  strategies  have  a  significant  impact  on
the performance of anomaly detection based on isolation
mechanisms. Current optimization techniques are mainly
for  tree-based  models.  Additionally,  most  partitioning
methods are unsupervised, ignoring any prior knowledge
or expert feedback. It is worth exploring how to optimize
the splitting method using limited labeled data to achieve
better detection.
 8.2.4   Extending isolation mechanisms to open-set
recognition (OSR)
OSR  is  an  emerging  field  in  machine  learning  that
aims to identify instances from previously unseen classes
during  testing[105, 106],  posing  challenges  for  conventional
anomaly detection methods that typically treat all devi-
ations as anomalies. The isolation mechanism can be ex-
tended  to  OSR  by  incorporating  class-specific  informa-
tion,  allowing  it  to  distinguish  unknown  classes  from
known ones and enable further detection within the un-
known  classes.  Furthermore,  integrating  isolation  mech-
anisms with deep learning representations offers a prom-
ising direction for improving OSR performance, as high-
lighted in recent surveys[107].
 9   Conclusions
Anomaly  detections  based  on  isolation  mechanisms,
which rely on the principle of isolating anomalies through
random partitioning, have emerged as a novel and effect-
ive  approach  for  identifying  anomalies  in  data.  These
methods  have  demonstrated  their  effectiveness  and  effi-
ciency  in  addressing  challenges  associated  with  large-
scale,  high-dimensional  and  heterogeneous  datasets.  By
leveraging the concept of isolating anomalies through ran-
dom partitioning, these methods offer significant advant-
ages, including low computational complexity, scalability
and robustness to noise and irrelevant features.
This survey provides a comprehensive review of state-
of-the-art isolation-based methods, covering key partition-
ing  strategies,  anomaly-scoring  techniques  and  al-
gorithmic  innovations.  In  addition,  their  applications
across  diverse  domains,  such  as  streaming  data,  traject-
ory  analysis  and  time  series  are  thoroughly  explored.
Moving forward, addressing open challenges, such as op-
timizing partitioning strategies and developing increment-
al learning capabilities, will be essential for further enhan-
cing the utility and impact of isolation-based methods.

Y. Cao et al. / Anomaly Detection Based on Isolation Mechanisms: A Survey
865
Abstract: Anomaly detection is a longstanding and active research area that has many applications in domains such as finance, secur- ity and manufacturing. However, the efficiency and performance of anomaly detection algorithms are challenged by the large-scale, high- dimensional and heterogeneous data that are prevalent in the era of big data. Isolation-based unsupervised anomaly detection is a novel and effective approach for identifying anomalies in data. It relies on the idea that anomalies are few and different from normal instances, and thus can be easily isolated by random partitioning. Isolation-based methods have several advantages over existing methods, such as low computational complexity, low memory usage, high scalability, robustness to noise and irrelevant features, and no need for prior knowledge or heavy parameter tuning. In this survey, we review the state-of-the-art isolation-based anomaly detection methods, includ- ing their data partitioning strategies, anomaly score functions, and algorithmic details. We also discuss some extensions and applica- tions of isolation-based methods in different scenarios, such as detecting anomalies in streaming data, time series, trajectory and image datasets. Finally, we identify some open challenges and future directions for isolation-based anomaly detection research.
